UX Case Study  ·  Ordestra  ·  Warehouse Management System

Designing for a warehouse floor, not a desk.

Ordestra runs the pick, pack, and dispatch operation behind e-commerce order fulfillment. The user isn't sitting at a monitor. They're moving through aisles with a scanner in one hand.

01

Context & the problem

Confirmed premise

Ordestra (WHMS) exists to run the physical side of order fulfillment for e-commerce sellers, and it replaced a manual, paper based process. This project was the digitization of that process end to end: getting the right item off the right shelf, into the right box, onto the right courier, without a printed sheet or a whiteboard in sight.

  • The core challenge wasn't information density. It was speed and error prevention under physical, time-pressured conditions, now made harder by the fact that going digital had to feel faster than paper, not slower.
  • Multiple staff work the same pipeline simultaneously: several picklists being picked at once, several totes being packed at once, several carriers being dispatched at once. A manual system had no way to show that in real time.
  • A single wrong pick or mislabeled box costs real money and a real customer complaint, so the interface has to make the correct action the obvious one, every time, the same job a good paper checklist used to do, just faster and traceable.
Where I'm still filling gaps

You confirmed this was a manual to digital project, which is the real premise now driving this whole case study. The specific manual tools shown above (paper picklists, whiteboards, phone coordination) are my informed guess at what "manual" looked like in a warehouse context, not your documented before state. Research: what going digital had to fix

Assumption. Confirm or replace

No formal research documents were shared for this project, so what follows is a structured, informed account of the kind of signals a manual to digital warehouse project typically surfaces, not a transcript of real sessions.

Manual process What it actually cost Digital response
Paper picklist per order No record of who picked what, or when Picklist cards with live pending or picked counts, tied to a named picker
Whiteboard tally at packing stations Erased and rewritten constantly, no shared visibility Per station progress bars and pending or packed counts, visible to everyone at once
Phone calls to confirm carrier pickup Slow handoff, manual recount right before pickup Carrier grouped dispatch view with one manifest, printed on demand
No single source of order status Support couldn't answer "where is this order" without walking the floor Orders dashboard tracing one order from items to shipment, AWB number, and delivery date

03

Two very different users, one system

Assumption. Confirm personas

The same product has to serve someone standing on a warehouse floor mid shift and someone sitting at a desk reconciling an order dispute. Those two contexts pull the interface in opposite directions.

04

The fulfillment pipeline

From your screens

An order moves through four stages, and the interface tracks it under a different name at each one, matching the language warehouse staff actually use rather than a single generic "order" label forced across every screen.

05

The end-to-end journey

Assumption. Confirm or replace

Zooming out from individual screens: this is what happens across all five stages, including the emotional arc, from the moment a picklist is created to the moment a courier picks it up.

The pattern across all five stages

Every pain point sits at a handoff between roles, not inside a single person's task. A supervisor sizing a picklist has no feedback from the picker who finishes it. A picker has no priority signal across active lists. A packer gets no size guidance from data the system already holds. The fix isn't per screen, it's making information one role already has visible to the next role who needs it.

Where I'm filling gaps with judgment

This map is built from what the screens imply about each role's task and from common floor operation patterns, not from real interviews or shadowing sessions. If you have real quotes, timing data, or observed friction from actual pickers or packers, send them over and I'll rebuild this map around your real evidence.

06

User flow: every path, including the loops

From your screens

The journey map shows the emotional shape of the process. This flow shows the actual decision logic underneath it, including the two places where the system has to send someone back a step rather than forward.

  • The picking loop repeats until every bin on the list is cleared, matching how a picker actually moves through the floor rather than assuming one pass is enough.
  • The contents check before printing a label is the one place the flow deliberately sends someone backward, because a wrong label printed once is far more expensive to fix than one extra verification step.
  • The "start now" decision at Ready to Pick reflects that pickers, not the system, choose which of several assigned lists to work first, since only they know the floor in real time.
07

Picking: speed with a paper trail

Your shipped screens

Multiple picklists run in parallel, each with its own progress. The design goal was to make "what's left to do, and where" answerable at a glance, from across the room.

08

Packing: where physical and digital have to match exactly

Your shipped screens

Packing is where a mistake becomes expensive: the wrong box dimensions, the wrong carrier, or the wrong item count means a return, a refund, or an angry customer. The form on the right does double duty as a checklist and a shipping label generator.

09

Dispatch: handing off to the carrier

Your shipped screens

The final stage groups work by carrier rather than by order, because that's how a dispatch operator actually has to think: everything going out with Delhivery today, everything going out with Bluedart today.

10

One system, reused everywhere

The list plus work columns layout isn't redesigned per stage. It's the same structural pattern from Ready to Pick through Dispatch, with only the content changing.

Why this mattered

Warehouse staff often rotate between stations. A picker moved onto a packing shift doesn't have to learn a new interface shape, just new content inside a shape they already know. That's a training time and error rate argument, not just a visual consistency one.

11

The back office: the Orders dashboard

Your shipped screens

A completely different mode: dense, tabular, built for someone auditing a specific order rather than moving through a physical pipeline.

13

Reflection

Draft. Confirm or replace

What I'd want to test

Real time on task data comparing a trained picker against a first shift picker, to see whether the reused layout pattern actually reduces onboarding time as intended.

A constraint worth naming

Designing for a shared warehouse terminal, not a personal device, changes assumptions about session length, interruption, and how forgiving the UI needs to be of someone walking away mid task.

What I'd revisit

Whether the vocabulary shift from Picklist to PickBin to Tote to Shipment, which matches warehouse speech, is actually intuitive to a brand new hire in week one, or only to staff who already know the floor.

What held up well

The single reused layout pattern across four very different stages: a strong systems decision that a sole designer could maintain consistently without a larger team.
